newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan cautious on mixing banks and commerce.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan cautious on mixing banks and commerce.

text.p: With Congress considering several proposals to modernize U.S. banking laws, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan signaled on Thursday the Fed is opposed to an approach that would immediately permit unlimited combinations between financial and commercial companies.

Greenspan, acknowledging that distinctions between the two spheres are already eroding, said, "Nonetheless, the (Federal Reserve) Board has concluded that it would be wise to move with caution in addressing the removal of the current legal barriers between commerce and banking."

The Clinton administration is considering including in its bank reform proposal, due in late March, a provision allowing unlimited mergers of commercial and financial firms. A task force headed by Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke endorsed that approach in a report now before Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, people familiar with the report said.

In prepared testimony for a House Banking subcommittee hearing, Greenspan said the Fed favors a transitional approach allowing financial companies to own a "small basket" of non-financial assets, set as a percentage limit of a firm's total assets or capital. Greenspan did not specify what the percentage limit should be.
One bill under consideration, introduced by New Jersey Republican Rep Marge Roukema, would allow financial companies to do 25 percent of their business in non-financial activities.
A bill proposed this week by Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato would go farther, permitting unlimited combinations of financial and commercial companies.
More generally, Greenspan said the Federal Reserve is strongly in favor of breaking down the Depression-era laws separating banking from other strictly financial activities.

"We strongly urge an extensive increase in the activities permitted to banking organizations and other financial institutions provided these activities are financed at non- subsidized market rates and do not pose unacceptable risks to our financial system," Greenspan said in his prepared testimony.

To avoid allowing banks to gain an unfair advantage from federal deposit insurance, therefore, Greenspan said banks should not be allowed to conduct new activities in direct subsidiaries. Rather, new activities should be conducted as offshoots of holding companies that also own banks.
"While a level playing field requires broader powers, it does not require subsidized ones," Greenspan added.

The Fed has seen that problems in a subsidiary can spread to other parts of a company, the central banker said. "Our experience has been that a problem in one legal entity can have a contagion effect on other entities," he said.
"Better safe than sorry," he added in explaining his opposition to allowing new activities at the subsidiary level.
